extracted.intended_audience: law students, legal practitioners, and scholars studying UK copyright and periodical publication law (historic statutes and case law)
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory legal treatise guidance on the regulation, stamp duties, property rights, evidence rules, and procedures applicable to periodical publications, pamphlets, newspapers, and related musical/ dramatic works under UK law (c.18–c.19th-century statutes and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of smaller political pamphlets/newspapers (60 Geo. III. c. 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pamphlets and papers containing public news, intelligence, or occurrences, or remarks thereon, or in any matter in church or state, printed in the united kingdom for sale, and published periodically, or in parts, or numbers, at intervals not exceeding twenty-six days; where any of them respectively shall not exceed two sheets (being not less than twenty-one inches in length, and seventeen inches in breadth, of which the cover forms no part), or shall be published for sale for less than sixpence, exclusive of the duty imposed by that act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such papers are to be deemed to be within the 38 Geo. III. c. 78. and other acts of parliament relating to newspapers; the definition affects which statutory duties and penalties apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of publication — recognizance or bond requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: No person, after thirty days from 5th Dec. 1819, is to be allowed to publish a news‑paper or any such pamphlets ... until he has entered into a recognizance before a Baron of the Exchequer; or has executed and delivered to some neighbouring justice of the peace, a bond to the King—with two or three sureties in three hundred pounds, if such newspaper is printed in London, or within twenty miles; and in two hundred pounds, if printed elsewhere, and his sureties in a like sum in the whole; conditioned for the payment of such penalty as may be imposed on publishing any blasphemous or seditious libel, under a penalty of twenty pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pre‑condition to lawful publication for certain pamphlets/newspapers; amounts of security vary by place of printing (London/within 20 miles vs elsewhere) and condition the publisher's liability for libels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surety rules — payment, bankruptcy, withdrawal, and replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: If a surety has paid the whole or part of the penalty in the recognizance or bond, or has become bankrupt, or has been discharged as an insolvent debtor, the person for whom he was bound must not publish any newspaper, &c. until he has ... entered into a new recognizance or bond, with sureties, in the same manner, and to the same amount as before, under a penalty of twenty pounds. A surety may withdraw himself on giving twenty days' notice in writing to the commissioners of stamps, and to the persons for whom he is surety; and at the expiration of such notice he will only be liable for penalties previously incurred. The person for whom such surety was bound must not publish any newspaper, &c. until he has entered into a new recognizance or bond, under a penalty of twenty pounds. This bond is not subject to any stamp duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism ensures continuous security; withdrawal permitted with notice but publisher must replace surety before continuing publication or face penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of copies to commissioners of stamps
rubrics_metrics.description: A pamphlet, the day on which it is published, or within six days, must be delivered to the commissioners of stamps, signed by the printer or publisher, with his name and place of abode (which is to be kept and paid for by the commissioners) under a penalty of one hundred pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If commissioners refuse to receive or pay for a copy on account of its not appearing within the act, they must, if required, deliver to the printer or publisher a certificate that a copy has been duly offered; the certificate exempts the printer/publisher from penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed price and date requirement on pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon every such pamphlet must be printed the price at which it is published for sale, and the day on which it is first published. The day which must be on the first day of every month, or within two days before or after it, under a penalty of 20£.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the publisher or any person who within two months after the day of publication printed thereon sells any such pamphlets on which the price printed shall be sixpence, or above that sum, by a less price than sixpence, he will forfeit 20£; this rule does not extend to the allowances made by the publisher to dealers or to a distributor by retail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content‑based legal treatment of smaller pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: If the contents of the smaller pamphlets are of a literary nature, quite distinct from any thing political or blasphemous, then the authors are subject only to the laws that affect the contents of the larger pamphlets, or (except the stamp duty) to the law of periodical publications in general. But the author of smaller pamphlets which contain any seditious libels, or blasphemy, are punished in a peculiar manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes regulatory and penal treatment of pamphlets by subject‑matter; political or seditious content invokes special penalties and rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty on advertisements (wrappers/parts) — security before stamps
rubrics_metrics.description: For every advertisement contained in or published on the wrapper of any periodical publication, or with any part or number of any book, or literary work published in parts or numbers, a duty of three shillings and sixpence is imposed; and no stamps are to be delivered out for pamphlets until security has first been given for payment of the duty of the advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever a work is published in parts, the first number must be entered at the stamp office so that duties (advertisement duty included) may be collected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty on newspapers and discount rules
rubrics_metrics.description: That duty is now four pence on every newspaper: but a discount of 20 per cent is allowed for prompt payment of any sum of 10£ or upwards, when the price of the paper does not exceed sevenpence; and 4 per cent to those who sell for a higher price than sevenpence. The newspaper must be marked to show that the discount is allowed, and the price of it must be printed on it. A penalty of 20£ is inflicted on those who sell it for more than the printed price.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discounts and marking requirements govern stamp revenue accounting; failure to comply leads to monetary penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Penalties for unstamped newspapers and related offences
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several penalties respecting newspapers: 20£ for printing and publishing, or for having possession of them, and 100£ for sending them out of the kingdom. And whoever sells newspapers or pamphlets unstamped may be sent to the House of Correction for any time not exceeding three months, whilst the informer is entitled to a reward of 40s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penalties apply to printers, possessors, senders abroad, and sellers of unstamped papers; enforcement includes fines, imprisonment, and informer rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty on sheets/contents and delivery of a printed copy
rubrics_metrics.description: On every sheet of any kind of paper contained in one copy of a pamphlet of the larger kind, and of the literary smaller ones, a duty of three shillings is imposed. One printed copy of every such pamphlet must be sent within six days after publication to the office of stamps, if it be published in London; if in the country, then it must be taken to a collector of stamps within fourteen days, or all persons concerned with it will be liable to forfeit 20£, and all costs of each suit; and a like penalty will be inflicted upon every person who sells it without the name and place of abode of the publisher being printed upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely deposit of a copy and clear imprinting of publisher details are mandatory; failure attracts monetary and procedural sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smaller political pamphlets treated like newspapers for duties and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The smaller political pamphlets are subjected to the same stamp duties as on newspapers, with the same allowances and discounts, and subject to all rules and regulations respecting newspapers. But they are to be free from the duties on the old or large pamphlets, and any person selling such pamphlet unstamped is rendered liable to a penalty of 20£.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification as 'smaller political pamphlet' places work within newspaper regulatory regime except as to certain pamphlet duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions from duties on newspapers/pamphlets
rubrics_metrics.description: The works exempted from the duties on newspapers and the pamphlets made newspapers are — acts of parliament, proclamations, orders of council, forms of prayer and thanksgiving, and acts of state ordered to be printed by his Majesty; printed votes or other matters by order of either House of Parliament; books commonly used in the schools of Great Britain; books containing only matters of devotion or piety; any paper containing a single advertisement printed and dispersed separately; daily accounts or bills of goods imported and exported, and the weekly bills of mortality, provided such bills or accounts do not contain any other matter than what hath been usually comprized therein. And also any work reprinted and republished in parts or numbers, whether wholly reprinted or abridged; provided the work was first printed and published two years before the reprinting and republication, and was not first published in parts or numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific classes of documents are carved out from duties; reprints meet exemption criteria only if original publication was at least two years earlier and not originally issued in parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in periodical publications — title/form/mode protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Although generally two books may bear the same title, yet there is a property in the name given to a periodical publication. It has been decided that the title, form, and mode of publication of a magazine cannot be imitated in such a manner as would necessarily mislead the public, and induce them to purchase the latter work instead of the continuing parts of the former one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts protect the overall presentation that would mislead purchasers; however publication under a similar though not the same title is lawful if the latter is distinct and nothing has been done to injure the sale of the former.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondents' communications are the property of addressee
rubrics_metrics.description: The communications from correspondents to the editors or proprietors of periodical publications are of course the property of the person to whom they are directed; and cannot be published by any other person, who by chance may have obtained possession of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial privilege/ownership protects submitted materials from third‑party publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in pamphlet and newspaper (personalty and assignability)
rubrics_metrics.description: The property in a pamphlet is exactly the same as that in a common book. The property in a newspaper is personal, and may be dealt with like all other personalty. It may, however, be useful to collect the cases that relate particularly to them. It may be devised. The interest in a newspaper, although of a fluctuating nature, comes within the meaning of 'goods and chattels' in the bankruptcy statutes; and therefore passes by the assignment of the commissioners, if the proprietor become a bankrupt. And if the printer and publisher of a newspaper assign his interest in it to a creditor as a security, but continues to print and publish as before, and no affidavit of the change of interest has been delivered to the commissioners of stamps, and he become bankrupt, the right to the paper will pass to his assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper ownership is treated as personal property for testamentary and bankruptcy purposes; formal notification (affidavit to commissioners) is relevant to third‑party rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and powers of justices in newspaper offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Two justices of the peace may hear and determine offences against the 10 Ann. c. 19 in relation to pamphlets and newspapers, on complaint made within three months, and on conviction, either on view or information, they may issue warrants for levying the penalties on the goods of the offender, and cause sale to be made if they are not redeemed in six days; and, in default of goods, they may commit the offender to prison. An appeal is given to justices at sessions, who are finally to determine the same; and, in case of conviction, issue warrants. The justices may mitigate the penalty, so that they do not reduce it lower than one‑fourth part above the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary remedy before two justices is a primary enforcement mechanism for statutory newspaper/pamphlet penalties; mitigation powers limited by costs floor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizance condition — good behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be made a part of the condition of the recognizance of a person, held to bail for publishing a libel, that he shall be of good behaviour during the continuance of the recognizance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizance can include behavioural conditions as a preventive measure against further libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on penalties recoverable before justices
rubrics_metrics.description: All penalties imposed by 60 Geo. III. c. 9. are to be recovered before any two justices of the peace of the county, &c. where the offence is committed: but no larger amount in the whole than one hundred pounds can be recovered before justices of peace, for penalties incurred in one day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory cap restricts summary recovery by justices in a single day to £100; larger sums require higher forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary procedure: summons, oath, judgment, and commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Two justices, in all cases in which they are authorized to determine offences against that act, upon complaint made within three months after the offence, may summon the party accused, and the witnesses; and, upon appearance or contempt of the party in not appearing, they may examine the witnesses on oath, and give judgment for the penalties incurred; and, in case the penalties are not immediately paid, may commit the offender for a time not exceeding six months, unless such penalties are sooner paid. The party convicted may, on giving security, to the amount of the penalties adjudged together with such costs as may be awarded in case judgment is affirmed, appeal to the next quarter or general sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides procedural detail for enforcement and appeal from justices to sessions; security for appeal must cover penalties and potential costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness penalties for non‑attendance or refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses summoned to attend before the justices, either for the prosecutor or the person accused, neglecting to attend, or appearing and refusing to give evidence, without a reasonable excuse, are liable to forfeit twenty pounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures witness compliance in summary proceedings; monetary sanction significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: No writ to remove orders/convictions under the newspaper acts
rubrics_metrics.description: No order or conviction, made under the acts respecting newspapers by any justices of peace, can be removed by any writ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates limited availability of extraordinary writ remedies (e.g., certiorari) to challenge justices' orders under these statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on who may commence actions for statutory penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: It is enacted that no person shall commence any action or information in any of his majesty's courts, or before any justices of peace, for any penalty under those acts, unless in the name of the Attorney‑General in England or Ireland, or the Lord Advocate in Scotland, or in the name of the solicitor or some other officers of the stamp duties in England, Scotland, or Ireland. All other actions, &c. are declared to be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralises enforcement of statutory penalties in Crown or authorised stamp officers; private prosecutions for these statutory penalties are barred unless brought by the named officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence rule: stamp‑office affidavit and matching newspaper conclusive
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been decided that the affidavit left at the stamp office, and a newspaper answering the whole description contained in that affidavit, produced by a person from the stamp office, is evidence, not only of the publication of the paper, but that it took place in the county in which it is described as having been printed; and that the provisions in the 11th section, which make it unnecessary to prove that the newspaper to which the trial relates was purchased at any house, apply to plaintiffs in civil suits, and prosecutors in criminal offices, as well as to persons seeking to recover penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory affidavit scheme greatly simplifies proof of publication and place; a certified copy of the affidavit and matching paper is sufficient evidence to support counts of composing/printing/publishing a libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificate/jurat authority proof
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to the certificate, if it does not appear in the jurat that the person, before whom it was made, had authority to take it, proof must be adduced that he had such power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical evidentiary requirement: absence of jurat detail may be cured by proof of authority to take the affidavit/certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternate modes of proving publication (pre‑statute practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before the passing of 38 Geo. III. c. 78 other modes had been resorted to in order to connect persons with the publication of newspapers. Thus it was considered sufficient evidence that a person was the publisher of a newspaper, when it was proved, that it was sold at his office, and that he, as proprietor of the paper, had given a bond to the stamp‑office ... And the publication of a newspaper was sufficiently proved by the evidence of the printer, who said that it was published in the usual way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where statutory affidavit evidence is unavailable, circumstantial proof such as sale at publisher's office, bond to stamp office, and printer's testimony can establish publication; unstamped newspapers may be read in evidence notwithstanding stamp penalty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of defendant to read extracts to explain or mitigate libel
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain the libel, and to mitigate the damages, the defendant has a right to have read in evidence extracts from a different part of the same newspaper, connected with the subject of the libellous passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows contextual evidence to be admitted for mitigation/explanation of alleged libelous passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chancery bill for discovery of anonymous proprietors/authors
rubrics_metrics.description: If a person has been libelled in a newspaper, and suspects the author to be a proprietor not named in the affidavit, he may file a bill in Chancery for a discovery of the names of any persons concerned in it. The defendants are not allowed to plead or demur, but must make the discovery required. Such information, when obtained, cannot however be used in any other proceeding, except in that for which the discovery is made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable remedy to compel disclosure of anonymous authors/proprietors where affidavit does not name them; discovery use limited to that proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical compositions treated as books under statute of 8 Anne
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical compositions are books to be protected by the statute of 8 Anne, and those acts of parliament which have enlarged the benefits to be derived from it. A piece of music published on a single sheet of paper is protected; and it is not material whether the matter pirated be a whole book of music, or some one tune of a particular name in a work bearing a different title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composer's property in a musical composition is the same as that in a book; protection extends to single tunes and to pieces printed on single sheets; the usual principles of assignment and piracy apply.
